# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

# The strongest document so far, though its arithmetic tells a different story from its mediation analysis

## The arithmetic

The main figures check out:

| Check | Calculation | Paper |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets, 24 months | 0.966 ÷ 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, system logs, 24 months | 0.966 ÷ 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden continuing organisations: hours | 34.9 ÷ 40.3 = 0.866 | −13.4% ✓ |
| Halden continuing organisations: per hour | 96.8 ÷ 0.866 = 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% ✓ |
| Decline, timesheet measure | 12.5% → 9.8% (about 22% smaller) | "about a quarter" ✓ |

The county's staffing cost estimate is plausible but rests on an unstated assumption. Twelve percent more staff would restore output to about 0.886 × 1.12 ≈ 99% of control. If staff were the only cost, cost per contact would rise about 13%. The quoted 9% implies staff costs are roughly 70% of the total.

## What the report does well

It answers most of the open questions from the earlier documents:

- **Unrecorded work.** System log hours were added, and they show slightly more work than timesheets. This answers my concern about unclaimed overtime.
- **Meeting time now has a baseline:** 7.4 → 3.9 hours in treated offices, 7.2 → 7.0 in control. This fixes the gap in the nine-month exploratory analysis.
- **Mediation was registered before the outcomes were known**, with two named mediators and one outcome.
- **Decay is tested within the same offices over time**, using the same measure, as I suggested for the meta-analysis.
- **The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is rebutted on its own terms.** All four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That makes the rebuttal decisive.
- **The Varga–Holm "entirely an artifact" claim is rebutted using their own standards:** record-based output, measured hours, a randomised comparison and at least 18 months.
- **The control offices' meeting audit is reported honestly as an unplanned observation**, and the report states plainly what the trial cannot tell us.
- **The Halden survivors are labelled "survivors twice over"** and treated as an upper bound.

## Problems

### 1. Simple accounting suggests meetings explain nearly all of the gain, not 47%

The calendar and timesheet figures can be combined directly. As a back-of-envelope difference-in-differences:

| Item | Change, treated vs control |
|---|---|
| Total hours (timesheets): −12% of about 37.9 | about −4.5 hours/week |
| Recurring meetings: −3.5 treated vs −0.2 control | about −3.3 hours/week |
| **Non-meeting hours** | **about −1.2 hours/week, roughly −4%** |
| Output per FTE | −3.4% |
| **Output per non-meeting hour** | **roughly 0%** |

Assume meetings produce no case output directly. Then nearly the entire per-hour gain is the removal of meeting time. Staff are about as productive per hour of non-meeting work as before; they simply spend fewer hours in meetings.

This matters for interpretation. The gain is real and valuable for the employer. But it is mainly a change in **how time is spent**, not people **working faster** in the time they spend on cases. That leaves little room for the 18% fatigue share.

The registered mediation estimate (47%) comes from a different calculation: a model of variation between offices. The gap between the two methods needs explaining. Either the model under-attributes the effect to meetings, or freed meeting time was not all spent on cases.

### 2. It's unclear what the log measure counts

The log measure is described as recording "time staff are working on cases". If that's literal, it excludes meetings. Then the 11% fall in log hours would mean case time fell 11%. The calendar arithmetic above implies case time fell only about 3–4%. These are inconsistent.

If logs do include meetings or general logged-in time, the description is loose. Since the mediation outcome is output per log-measured hour, the report needs to say exactly what the denominator includes.

### 3. Mediation "confirms" more than a single test of 14 offices can

- **The data aren't independent.** The meetings hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices. Registering the test at month 11 rules out choosing the analysis after the 24-month results were known. It doesn't make this an independent replication.
- **The intervals look too narrow.** The reference to "a larger sample of office-months" is a warning sign. Repeated months from the same office aren't independent observations, so the effective sample is 14 offices. A 28–66% interval for a mediated share with 14 clusters is hard to get with properly clustered inference. The report should state how it calculated the intervals.
- **The key assumption isn't met by randomisation.** Mediators aren't randomised, so the analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediator and outcome. The Limitations section acknowledges this, but the Summary still says "confirms".

"Is supported by" would match the evidence.

### 4. The decline is overstated in the Summary and confounded

- **The Summary compares different measures.** It reports a fall "from 12.5% to 8.5%", but the 12.5% is timesheet-based and the 8.5% is log-based. Like for like, the fall is 12.5% → 9.8%. The body gets this right; the Summary doesn't.
- **The decline isn't statistically established.** The intervals overlap heavily: 6.9–18.4 at nine months and 4.6–15.2 at 24 months. "Consistent with some fading" is fair; "has declined" is stronger than the data.
- **The control group improved.** Two of the seven control offices cut meetings and raised output per hour by 4.1%. Averaged over all control offices, that is roughly 1.2 points. That alone could explain close to half of the 2.7-point narrowing. Part of the apparent "decay" may be control offices catching up, not treated offices fading. This also means the 24-month difference-in-differences slightly *understates* the effect of the treatment.
- **The control meeting figures need checking.** If two offices fell to 5.0 hours, a control average of 7.0 requires the other five to average about 7.8, up from roughly 7.2. That's possible, perhaps from weighting by staff numbers, but it should be explained.

### 5. The Halden follow-up is framed more favourably than its data

- **The reversions are mischaracterised.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". One was a **marketing agency citing client deadlines**, which the meta-analysis's coding would class as discretionary work. So the reversions don't divide cleanly by coverage. That is relevant to the sector question and should be reported plainly.
- **Responders are another selected group.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded, on top of the selection already discussed. Responding organisations were probably the ones with good news.
- **The original misreporting goes unacknowledged.** A Halden author is on this team, yet the report doesn't acknowledge that Halden misreported its attrition, which Varga–Holm documented. It should.
- **Time tracking still misses unrecorded work.** The Halden hours come from time-tracking software, not system logs. That is the same gap the Varden team just closed for its own data.

### 6. Smaller points

- **Sick days (−27%).** The report still doesn't say whether rotas meant fewer days or shorter days, so the mechanical share of the fall is still unknown.
- **Resignations** (4.1% v 7.9%) are raw levels, not difference-in-differences, with no interval.
- **The counter arm** ended at month 12, so the clearest result on coverage-bound work has no long-run data. That's reasonable given the waiting times, but worth stating in the Limitations.
- **Quality held steady** (3.2% v 3.0% overturned on appeal), which is reassuring.

## Overall

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| A per-hour gain persists at 24 months in case-processing | Well supported (8.5%, CI 3.4–13.8, randomised, log hours) |
| Output per employee is mostly maintained | Fair (−3.4%, CI −8.0 to +1.2; a loss of up to 8% isn't excluded) |
| The gain has declined | Possible; the intervals overlap and the decline is confounded by control offices improving |
| Meetings account for 47% of the gain | Supported as a model estimate; simple accounting suggests closer to all of it |
| Fatigue accounts for 18% | Weak, given the accounting and the untestable assumption |
| The meta-analysis's "no decay" claim is unsupported | Well supported |
| "Entirely an artifact" is refuted | Well supported |
| Halden reversions all reflect coverage obligations | Not accurate (the marketing agency) |

Across all five documents, the evidence now looks like this:
- Reduced hours in backlog-type work yield roughly a 8–10% gain in output per actual hour, lasting at least two years. Output per employee is slightly down.
- That gain seems to come largely from cutting meetings rather than from rest.
- In coverage-bound work, reduced hours reduce output and service unless staff are added.

The open question is the one the report itself names. Could a meeting audit without cutting hours capture most of the gain, or is the cut in hours what forces the reorganisation to happen and last? A trial with a "reorganise only" arm would answer it.
